body.hook: Integrity is often described as doing the right thing even when no one is watching. Honesty and integrity are what make people trust you, and trust, once broken, is hard to rebuild.

study.title: Honest to the Core
study.question: What do honesty and integrity mean, and why do they matter?
study.passage:
Key ideas (written for this lesson):
Honesty is about the truth of what we say and show. Integrity is wider: it means our actions match our values all the time, including keeping promises and doing our share.
Kinds of dishonesty: lying, exaggerating, leaving out important facts, cheating, taking credit for others' work, pretending to be someone else online.
Trust: like a bank account; honest actions are deposits, broken promises and lies are withdrawals. One big withdrawal can empty it.
Activities: 1. Spectrum line: students stand on a line from "always wrong" to "sometimes OK" for statements: telling a friend you like a gift you don't; copying a homework answer; not mentioning you got extra change at a store; telling a parent you finished homework when you didn't; keeping a promise even when it's inconvenient. Discuss reasons. 2. Integrity in action: describe a time (real or fictional) when someone did the right thing with no one watching. 3. Discuss: are white lies ever acceptable? What could you say instead that is both honest and kind?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

Discuss white lies and kind honesty

body.hook: Most people who cheat or lie don't think of themselves as dishonest. They tell themselves a story: "Everyone does it," "It's not a big deal," "The test was unfair." Spotting these rationalizations is the first step to resisting them.

study.title: Excuses and Truths
study.question: Why do people cheat or lie, and what harm does it cause?
study.passage:
Case studies (fictional, written for this lesson):
Case 1: Lina copies a paragraph from a website into her science report without quotation marks or a source because she ran out of time.
Case 2: Two friends split the questions on an individual take-home quiz and share answers.
Case 3: Ahmed asks an AI tool to write his English essay and submits it unchanged when the teacher allowed AI only for brainstorming.
Case 4: Priya's team gets credit for a project, but she knows one member did almost nothing. Should she tell the teacher?
Common rationalizations: "Everyone does it." "No one gets hurt." "I'll only do it once." "The teacher's rules are unfair." "I didn't have time."
Harms: you don't learn the skill; grades no longer show what you know; it's unfair to honest classmates; it damages trust between students and teachers; schools may apply consequences.
Activity: for each case, identify the dishonesty, the rationalization, who is harmed and a better choice (e.g. ask for an extension, cite the source, use AI as allowed and be transparent).
study.source: Original fictional cases written for this lesson.
discussion: Who is harmed when someone cheats?
Which case was hardest to judge, and why?
What would you do in Priya's position?
study.product: Analyze two cases in writing: the dishonesty, the rationalization, the harms and a better choice.

body.objective: Students will be able to practise accountability.
successCriteria: I can explain accountability and why it matters
I can give a sincere apology with the key parts
I can make a plan to repair harm
body.hook: Everyone makes mistakes. What shows character is what happens next: blaming others and making excuses, or owning it, apologizing and making it right. That's accountability.

vocabulary.definition: Taking responsibility for your actions and their effects.
A duty to do something or to care for something.
Expressing regret and responsibility for a wrong.
Making up for harm, such as replacing or fixing something.
Putting responsibility for your actions on others.
Believing you can learn and improve from mistakes.

study.title: Owning It
study.question: How do I take accountability for my mistakes?
study.passage:
Accountability guide (written for this lesson):
Accountable responses: admit what you did, acknowledge the effect on others, apologize sincerely, make it right, and change future behaviour.
Non-accountable responses: denying, blaming others ("he started it"), minimizing ("it was just a joke"), excuses ("I was tired"), non-apologies ("sorry if you were offended").
A sincere apology has: 1. "I'm sorry for..." (name the specific action). 2. "It was wrong because..." (show you understand the harm). 3. "To make it right, I will..." (repair). 4. "Next time, I will..." (change). 5. Optionally, "Will you forgive me?" without demanding it.
Role-plays (fictional): breaking a borrowed calculator; posting a mean comment about a classmate; forgetting your part of a group project; saying something hurtful in anger. Partners practise an accountable response and the listener describes how it felt.
Reflection: think of a mistake you made (keep private if you prefer); what would full accountability have looked like?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Learn the parts of a sincere apology
Reflect privately on a past mistake
discussion: Which part of an apology is hardest to say?
How did it feel to receive a sincere apology in the role-play?
study.product: Write a sincere apology for a fictional situation with all four parts, plus a restitution plan.
